record.label: A terminal convex-chord obstruction
record.statement: Let r<1 and q be C1 on [r,1), with q(r)=r, qprime(r)<=1, q<=1 and qprime strictly convex on (r,1). Then q(t)<t for r<t<1. A crossing forces qprime(t)>1 by strict trapezoid comparison; subsequent convex secants force q(s)>1 near 1. No derivative at one is used.
record.boundary: Ordinary authored deduction checked against retained mathematical inputs; no new Lean declaration, elaborated dependency, cross-model transport, Comparator acceptance or independent proof certification is asserted.

aligned_passages.text: **Theorem 5.1 (full support).** In the pure zero-field SK model with $\xi(t)=t^2/2$, let $\gamma\in\mathcal U$ minimize $\mathcal P$. Then $\operatorname{supp}\mu_\gamma=[0,1)$ and $\gamma$ is strictly increasing. For every associated diffusion started at zero, $\mathbb E u(t,X_t)^2=t$ and $\mathbb E a(t,X_t)^2=1$ for $0\le t<1$. Keep the same minimiser, diffusion and moment function $q$ throughout. Section 3 has established $G\ge0$, $G=0$ on the support $S=\operatorname{supp}\mu_\gamma$, and the contact conditions $q(s)=s$, $q'(s)\le1$ at support points. At zero, the value identity comes from symmetry, and the slope bound requires $0\in S$. Section 4 supplies curvature on constant intervals for every admissible coefficient. These premises are available before any support gap is excluded. We first deal with the endpoint at one, then use the curvature estimate on the remaining intervals. For a terminal interval $(a,1)$, including empty support $[0,1)$, the cusp estimate gives $1-q(t)\gtrsim\sqrt{1-t}$ and hence $G<0$ near one. On a positive plateau with two contact endpoints, strict convexity puts $q'$ below its endpoint chord, although its integral must equal the interval length. On a zero plateau the heat argument makes $q'$ strictly increasing, below the right contact slope. At an initial gap, use the one-sided contact slope if $0\in S$; otherwise the coefficient is zero and symmetry supplies $q(0)=0$. **Why a terminal plateau violates the variational inequality.** Suppose that $\gamma=c$ on $(a,1)$, where $0\le a<1$ and $c\ge0$ is finite. The endpoint $1$ is outside the support domain, so there is no contact condition there to complete an endpoint-chord argument. Instead we will prove $$ 1-q(t)\ge C\sqrt{1-t} \tag{5.1} $$ for some $C>0$ and every $t$ sufficiently close to one. The proof separates two facts: the diffusion puts positive probability density near zero, and the smoothed terminal slope has a definite deficit from $\pm1$ in a shrinking window around zero. Fix $s\in(a,1)$ and let $\rho_s$ be the law of $X_s$. Choose $R<\infty$ such that $p_0=\rho_s([-R,R])>0$. For $c>0$, set $$ h(t,y)=\mathbb E e^{c|y+\sqrt{1-t}Z|},\qquad \Phi(t,y)=c^{-1}\log h(t,y), $$ where $Z$ is standard normal. The drift on this interval is $c\Phi_x=h_x/h$, and the transition density is $$ k_{s,t}(x,y)=p_{t-s}(y-x)\frac{h(t,y)}{h(s,x)},\qquad p_v(z)=(2\pi v)^{-1/2}e^{-z^2/(2v)}. \tag{5.2} $$ The heat-semigroup identity normalises this kernel; equivalently, for Brownian motion started at $(s,x)$, $h(t,B_t)/h(s,x)$ is the positive mean-one change of measure which adds the drift $h_x/h$. For $c=0$, the same kernel formula applies with $h=1$, and the value function is the ordinary heat evolution of $|x|$. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 6.3, proof of (6.6)][fs-var]. Put $L=1-s$ and $\delta=L/2$. For $s+\delta\le t<1$, $|x|\le R$ and $|y|\le1$, $$ p_{t-s}(y-x)\ge (2\pi L)^{-1/2}e^{-(R+1)^2/(2\delta)}=:k_*>0, $$ while $h(t,y)\ge1$ and $h(s,x)\le e^{cR}\mathbb E e^{c\sqrt L|Z|}=:M<\infty$. Integrating (5.2) over the part of $\rho_s$ in $[-R,R]$ therefore gives a density $f_t$ of $X_t$ with $$ f_t(y)\ge p_0k_*/M=:m>0 \quad(s+\delta\le t<1,\ |y|\le1). \tag{5.3} $$ Only positive mass of a compact set was needed at time $s$; no density assumption on $\rho_s$ has entered. Now write $\varepsilon=1-t$ and restrict to $|y|\le\sqrt\varepsilon$. Differentiating the terminal heat formula gives, with the unweighted interpretation for $c=0$, $$ u(t,y)= \frac{\mathbb E[\operatorname{sgn}(y+\sqrt\varepsilon Z) e^{c|y+\sqrt\varepsilon Z|}]} {\mathbb E e^{c|y+\sqrt\varepsilon Z|}}. $$ The denominator is at most $D=e^c\mathbb E e^{c|Z|}<\infty$. Each sign has unnormalised mass at least $p_*:=\mathbb P(Z\ge1)>0$: the threshold $|y/\sqrt\varepsilon|$ is at most one, and the exponential weight is at least one. Hence each sign has tilted probability at least $\theta=p_*/D\in(0,1/2)$. It follows that $$ |u(t,y)|\le1-2\theta,\qquad 1-u(t,y)^2\ge4\theta(1-\theta)=:\kappa>0. $$ Multiplying this uniform deficit by the density lower bound (5.3) and the window width $2\sqrt\varepsilon$ yields $$ 1-q(t)=\int_{\mathbb R}(1-u(t,y)^2)f_t(y)\,dy \ge 2m\kappa\sqrt{1-t}. $$ This proves (5.1) with $C=2m\kappa$. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 6.3, density and terminal-window estimates][fs-var]. The sign of the contradiction is now explicit. For $s'$ sufficiently close to one, the estimate holds at every $t\in[s',1)$, so $$ \begin{aligned} G(s')&=\int_{s'}^1(q(t)-t)\,dt\\ &\le\frac{(1-s')^2}{2} -\frac{2C}{3}(1-s')^{3/2}<0. \end{aligned} $$ The final inequality holds once $\sqrt{1-s'}<4C/3$. It contradicts the nonnegative cost of adding an atom at $s'$. This proof covers $c=0$ as well as $c>0$. In particular, empty support is impossible: then $\mu_\gamma=0$ and $\gamma=0$ on all of $[0,1)$. The terminal-plateau conclusion was already recorded in [Auffinger, Chen and Zeng (2020), Remark 7][acz]; the estimates above supply the quantitative argument needed here. **A shorter qualitative exclusion.** The existing curvature input also excludes a terminal support gap without estimating its boundary layer. Here is the elementary calculus step. Suppose $q\in C^1([r,1))$, $q(r)=r$, $q'(r)\le1$, $q\le1$, and $q'$ is strictly convex on $(r,1)$. If $q(t)\ge t$ at some $r1$. For $t1. $$ Consequently $q(s)\ge t+(s-t)q'(t)>1$ for $s$ sufficiently close to one, a contradiction. Thus $q(t) First consider a gap $(a,b)$ with both endpoints in $S$, allowing $a=0$. Compact-strip regularity gives continuity of $q'$ on $[a,b]$, even if $\gamma$ jumps at an endpoint. Contact gives $$ q(a)=a,\qquad q(b)=b,\qquad q'(a),q'(b)\le1. \tag{5.4} $$ If the constant coefficient is $c>0$, Section 4 makes $q'$ strictly convex in the gap. Continuity extends the chord comparison to its endpoints, giving $$ q'(t)<\frac{b-t}{b-a}q'(a)+\frac{t-a}{b-a}q'(b)\le1, \qquad a0. $$ The first term is nonnegative; strict convexity makes the second positive. Only continuity of $q'$ is needed at the ends. For example, a jump $\Delta\gamma$ at $s$ gives the one-sided identity $$ q''(s+)-q''(s-)=-2\Delta\gamma\,\mathbb E a(s,X_s)^3. $$ It follows by applying Itô's formula to $a^2$ and using continuity of its derivative moments on a compact strip. Taking $\gamma=0$ before $s=1/2$ and $\gamma=1/2$ afterward makes this jump strictly negative; the terminal Cole–Hopf solution has positive Hessian. Thus continuity of $q'$ does not license classical higher time derivatives across coefficient jumps. [OpenAI (2026a), proof of Corollary 6.4][fs-density]. If $(0,b)$ is a gap and $0\in S$, the preceding proof applies using the one-sided contact slope bound at zero. Because $(0,b)$ contains no mass, the support condition at zero forces an atom there and hence $c=\gamma(0)>0$. Its absence has not been proved at this stage. If instead the complementary component is $[0,b)$ with $0\notin S$, there is no mass anywhere in $[0,b)$. Thus $\gamma=0$ there. The identity $q(0)=0$ comes from zero-field symmetry, and the right endpoint gives $q(b)=b$, $q'(b)\le1$. Here $q''(t)>0$ for $00 \qquad(0\le a0$ is already impossible: either $h\le1$ everywhere, forcing $h\equiv1$ by its integral, or it attains an interior maximum above one, where $h'=0$ and $h''\le0$. This is an elementary deduction from these premises. Chen's conditional crossing theorem, with its own hypotheses, is of this form; §4 proves the stronger $q'''>0$ throughout a positive plateau, without a minimizer premise. See [Chen, arXiv:2607.18032v1, Proposition 4.2 and the proof of Proposition 4.3][chen26]. Neither statement supplies terminal contact at the excluded endpoint one.

### 5.4 The remaining initial and terminal gaps **Initial gap with zero outside the support.** Suppose $[0,s)$ is missing and $s<1$ is the first support point. Then $\gamma=0$ there, so the positive-coefficient bound supplies no strictness. Instead the zero-coefficient heat identity gives $$ q''(t)=\mathbb E[\Phi_{xxx}(t,X_t)^2]>0\qquad(00$. To control a later slope, use the same chord rule on the larger interval $[r,s]$, where $t0. $$ Consequently $q(s)\ge t+(s-t)(1+h(t))$. Choose any time $$ t+\frac{1-t}{1+h(t)}0$, and the lower bound now gives $q(s)>1$, contradicting $q(s)\le1$ strictly before time one. Thus $q(t)[§5, terminal estimate](../long/reasoning-record.md#terminal-gap). [Auffinger–Chen–Zeng, Remark 7][acz] had already recorded the absence of terminal plateaus. These cases exhaust the complement of the support. Contact now gives $q(t)=t$ for every interior time, and symmetry includes zero. Differentiating gives $\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^2]=1$, completing the theorem.

### 7.4 Answers to the questions

**Question 1.** Adding mass at $1/2$ gives cumulative heights
$0,2,2+\varepsilon,3+\varepsilon$, in their successive intervals;
removing it at $1/4$ gives heights $0,2-\varepsilon,3-\varepsilon$.
Both functions remain nonnegative and nondecreasing. Removing mass at
$1/2$ instead lowers the height from $2$ to $2-\varepsilon$ there,
creating a downward jump, so it is forbidden even though all values
remain nonnegative. Scaling both weights preserves all admissibility
conditions. These tests concern allowed candidates; a smaller ordinary
area alone does not establish a smaller Parisi value.

**Question 2.** The state has accumulated variance $1/4$, so it is
distributed as $Z/2$. The remaining noise has variance $3/4$, and
its standard deviation in the value-slope formula is $\sqrt3/2$.
Thus

$$
q_0(1/4)=\int_{\mathbb R}
\left(2F_{\mathrm G}(z/\sqrt3)-1\right)^2\varphi(z)\,dz.
$$

The two variances agree at half time, but not here. For nonzero $z$,
the magnitude of the response is now smaller, so $q_0(1/4)<1/3$.
The arcsine formula in Section 7.1 also gives this comparison.

**Question 3.** A strictly convex $f'$ lies below its endpoint chord.
That chord has mean height $(1/2+3/2)/2=1$, hence integral three.
Therefore $f(5)-f(2)=\int_2^5f'(t)\,dt<3$, contradicting the
prescribed values. With non-strict convexity the data are possible:
$f(t)=2+(t-2)/2+(t-2)^2/6$ has affine derivative and satisfies all
four endpoint values. The argument needs a strict loss of area; the
common endpoint upper bound of one in Figure 2 is convenient, not essential. This is a
calculus example, not a candidate SK moment function.

**Question 4.** Since $q(r)=r$, reaching or passing the diagonal at
$t$ means $\int_r^t h\ge0$. Strict convexity places $h$ below its
endpoint chord, so that integral is less than
$(t-r)(h(r)+h(t))/2$. With $h(r)\le0$, this forces $h(t)>0$.
The chord rule on $[r,s]$, solved for $h(s)$, keeps every later value
at least $h(t)$. Integrating gives
$q(s)\ge t+(s-t)(1+h(t))>1$ for a suitable $s<1$, violating the
bound. If $q$ never reaches the diagonal, then $G(r)<0$ instead.
Thus both possibilities contradict the conditions on a minimiser.
